voice.text: Scoop up a handful of garden soil. [pause] What is really inside it? Just one thing, [pause] or a mix of many things? Tap your guess.

Soil is a <emphasis>mix</emphasis> of four ingredients. [pause] Tiny rock bits. [pause] Humus — dead leaves and plants that rotted into dark crumbs. [pause] Water. [pause] And air. Look close and you can find all four.

Nature makes soil <emphasis>slowly</emphasis>. [pause] Rain, ice and roots crumble big rock into tiny bits. Fallen leaves rot into humus. [pause] One handful of soil can take hundreds of years to make.

Underground, soil sits in layers. [pause] Topsoil on top — dark, soft, and the richest in humus. [pause] Lighter subsoil below. And solid rock at the very bottom. [pause] Plants do most of their feeding in the topsoil.

Soil does two jobs for plants. [pause] It <emphasis>holds</emphasis> them: roots grip the soil so wind cannot tip them over. [pause] And it <emphasis>feeds</emphasis> them: roots drink water and nutrients — plant food — right out of the soil.

And soil is a busy home. [pause] Worms, moles and roly-polys live in it — and they make it <emphasis>better</emphasis>! [pause] Worm tunnels let air and water in and mix the layers. The diggers are the soil's helpers.
Let's mix soil from scratch! [pause] For each card, tap: into the mix, or not soil.
Rock bits, humus, water, air — your soil mix is complete! [pause] Now stack the layers.
Now stack the underground layers, from the top down.
Topsoil, subsoil, solid rock — stacked! [pause] Last job: who helps the soil?
Is this good for the soil, or bad for it? Tap a button.
You know your soil! [pause] Now show what you know.
Not quite. Soil is not one thing — it is a recipe with four ingredients. Is this one of them?
Not quite. Ask: can it <emphasis>rot</emphasis> into food for the soil? Plastic never can.
Not quite. Remember: the dark, richest layer sits on top; the hard rock waits at the bottom.
Not quite. The diggers look messy — but their tunnels bring air and mix the soil.
Not quite. Dead leaves are not trash to the soil — they are tomorrow's humus.
Not quite. Soil is made slowly. What washes away is not replaced next week.
Not quite. Think about the four ingredients, and who helps them.
Yes! Crumbled rock is the gritty part of the mix. In it goes!
Yes! Rotted leaves become humus — the dark, food-rich part of soil.
Yes! Soil holds tiny drops of water between its crumbs.
Yes! Tiny air pockets hide between the crumbs — roots and worms breathe it.
Yes! Plastic never rots into food for the soil. It does not belong in the mix.
Yes! Topsoil on top — dark and richest, where plants feed.
Yes! Subsoil next — lighter, with fewer food crumbs.
Yes! Solid rock at the bottom — the soil's crumbly future!
Yes! Worm tunnels let air and water in and mix the soil. Worms are helpers!
Yes! Rotting leaves become humus — new plant food for the soil.
Yes! The mole's digging mixes and loosens the soil, like a tiny plow.
Yes! Chewed-up leaves rot faster — the roly-poly speeds up the humus.
Yes! Plastic never rots into food. It just sits there, in the way.
Yes! The richest layer is lost — and nature needs many, many years to remake it.
What is soil made of?
How long does nature take to make new soil?
Which layer is the richest for plants?
You find worms all over the garden bed. What should you do?
What does soil do for a plant?
You know what's under your feet! [pause] Well done.
Good try! Let's watch the soil recipe once more.
Lesson done! Now go dig a real cup of soil with a grown-up, and hunt for all four ingredients.
